title: Birth, early listening, first teachers and first bands (Hansberry, George Jones, Kid Rena)
summary: Born 1903 in the Battlefield area of New Orleans, he listened to Kid Rena and the Excelsior band, studied with Professor Hansberry and Baptiste Brown, played in George Jones's band, tried his own orchestra, then joined Rena's brass band; also memories of dance halls and Sun Allen and Celestin.

venues.name: Roof Garden of the Pythian Temple

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Dick Allen. I see. Where were you born, Richardson? In New Orleans. What section? They call it the battlefield. That's over around Lafayette and Cypress. Lafayette and Cypress. Yeah. You know I forgot to put today's date on this thing and what are we doing on it? See we're recording in the library in Seminar Room 2, Tulane University. And what's today's date? October the, I can't think. 29th I believe. October the 29th, 1960. So you were born around Cypress and Lafayette, that's your neighborhood? That's right. That's right. Where is Cypress? I can't place it. Cypress, it's uh, was just about two blocks on the downtown side of the New Basin Canal. Oh yeah. See. And what's the exact date of your birth? 18th of April. What year? 1903. 1903. 1903. Yeah. I see. Did you listen to music much before you played? Well, I did. I listened to Rainey most of the time, Kid Rainey. And they had a brass band they called Excelsa. I used to love to listen to them play parades. Mm-hmm. I see. And uh, did anybody in your family play music around the home? No, no. I was the only one. Mm-hmm. They sang? No. No, no. I thought maybe you picked up some talent through them somehow. No, I just brushed that up my own self. Mm-hmm. I see. Uh, when you started listening to Rainey and Excelsa, do you remember any of the guys in those different bands? Well, no. I can't remember anybody but Rainey now. Mm-hmm. That's been so long, I couldn't remember. How old were you when you started listening to Rainey? Well, I was about 17 years old. And when did you start following parades? Well, I guess I was about around my 20s because in those times, when you're around about 16 and 17 years old, old people were so close on you, you couldn't get out around those things. Mm-hmm. So I was around my teens when I started following parades. You couldn't sneak off when you were young. No, no. It wouldn't have to be your parent. It would be somebody else that would know you and it would be just as bad as your parent. Mm-hmm. You remember the guys in the Excelsior at all at that time? No, I can't remember. You don't remember the leader? The leader of the Excelsior? No. See? Well, when did you first start playing yourself? Well, I can't exactly call the time, but I was real young. I guess I was about in my 20s. About in my 20s when I started playing. We had Professor Hansberry. He was learning us. You remember his full name? No, I can't remember his full name. You started off with a teacher or started off playing by yourself? No, I started off with a teacher, Hansberry. And how did he teach you? Well, he was all right. I think he was a nice person. And that means a plenty when you know how to treat young people. That most encourages him. Well, did he have a method or did he start you out with his own stuff? Well, he did have some of his own stuff, but he would write it out. Write in music, make his own parts out that he wanted you to play, to learn you on. And that's how I did the start. Do you remember any of the little tunes he started you out on? Well, I believe about the first piece we learned how to play was Little Lies of Jane. Yeah, that's a old one I'm a. Did you play as a group when you first started or would he give you lessons by yourself? Well, he gave lessons to each one of us, about a month or two. And then we tried to organize a little band. We had Albert Brown playing drum, Charlie Lonzo playing guitar. And I can't remember the rest. Charlie Lonzo, is he left handed or right handed guitar player? He was right handed. Yeah, I got him confused with another fellow. I know a left handed guitar player named Charlie and I can't ever find out his name. But that's something you don't see very often, you know. Left handed. No, you very seldom see that. I haven't seen him in years. He used to play around with Noon and Sam, I guess it was. Well, this Charlie, what I'm telling you about, he's gone now. He's passed. How long? Good while. Oh yeah, he's been gone about fifteen, sixteen years. Well, that wouldn't be the same fellow. Because that was recent. How big a band did you have when you were playing? Well, we had about seven pieces. We had seven pieces. Did you read all your stuff? Oh yeah. Most of what we did was reading. Yeah. Like Liza Jane and those kind of numbers, well, it was by head. About how many head numbers did you have in all? Well, I had about three, about four. Had Summer These Days, Down By The Riverside. That was a hymn. We used to play it in jazz. Tipperary, a long ways from Tipperary. That's about all I can remember. About that time, who were some of the other trumpet players you listened to aside, Renee? And you were just getting started. Well, Buddy P.T. He was one of the old trumpet players. And there was another trumpet player, he learned me a good bit. His name was Baptiste Brown from Martin Carlton. He learned me a good bit. I'd go sometime and get him up out of his bed. He'd be asleep. Sit on the side of his bed to learn me. Was he a good reader? Yes, he was good. And how did he teach you? Did he use a method? Well, yes. But I'd forgotten the name of the method he had. And then he'd write manuscripts for me. Did you say whether Hanbury had a method or not at all? Or did he write it all out? I'm not sure. I think he did have a method, a book of some sort, but I can't place a name of it. Well, back to the other trumpet players. Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. Did Hanbury play in any bands himself? No, not as I know of. He was just an instructor at that time. And Bat Brown, what about him? He played with bands, didn't he? Bat... Bat... Bat... Bat... Batiste Brown? Oh, yeah. Batiste Brown used to play... I can't call the name of the band. Where did they play? Did they play steady in place? No, they mostly played parades. They mostly played parades. Well, when you got this little band organized, did you play any jobs for free or did you get money? Well, the most we did was we didn't sign any kind of contracts of any sort. We just would accept what was given. So it was mostly like free. Where did you play? Where did you play? Well... I'm trying to study. The last place I played was down on Claiborne Avenue. Claiborne and what? I forgot. It was on the back of town side of the bank. We used to play there every Sunday evening. About what neighborhood? No, I've forgotten. Uptown? Downtown. Down below Canal? Yeah, below Canal. It was about three blocks on the downtown side of Lision Field. Around Maroney in that neighborhood. Well, I wouldn't say exactly yes because I kind of confused those streets. Yeah. Well, anyway, did you get, how much would you get when they did pay you on the jobs like that, if you don't mind telling me when you're still? Well, we'd make sometimes three dollars, three or four dollars. Well, that's pretty good pay. And tips. That's three dollars in all or three dollars a man? Three dollars a man. Yeah. That's very good for those times. Okay. Then after that, what did you do? Well, by the way, whose band was that? I'm trying to, did they have any leader? Did you all just split it? Well, they mostly, no they didn't have a leader. It was George Jones' band. That early band? Yeah, George Jones. He was an old guitar player, sometime he'd play bass. Used to sing, comedian like. What would he sing? Old Lies of Jane was his favorite number. Do you have any funny songs other than that? No, I can't remember any other. Mm-hmm. Just those old numbers like Lies of Jane, Alabama Bomb, Long Waves from Tipperware, High Society, Tiger Rags. Mm-hmm. Let's see. Well, how long was that band up? Well, I couldn't exactly estimate the time. Mm-hmm. I was up about a year or two. Could have been about that long. Play any parades when you were? No. Not then. No. I didn't play any parades until I met Kid Rainey. Mm-hmm. Then he started taking me out on his jobs. Parade jobs? Parade jobs, uh-huh. Who would he have with his band? Well, Rainey would use, I can remember, George Lewis sometime, the clarinet player. Mm-hmm. And sometime Buddy P.T. That's the only three I can remember. Mm-hmm. Who would he have on snare drum? No, I can't remember his snare drum player. You don't remember drum, sir? No. If I'm not sure, I believe that was Rainey's brother, the drummer. Kid Rainey's brother. I guess it would be. Yeah. Uh, that reminds me, uh, you know who I saw up in the country a few months ago was, uh, Morris French. Morris French? Do you remember him, the trombone player? Yeah, it's been many years since I seen Morris, so I don't think I'd know Morris if I'd seen him. You know him. We took a ride up there with Punch, you know. Did you ever play with him? No, I never did play with him. Uh, what was your band after George Jones, after that first band? After George Jones? Well, I tried to organize an orchestra once, but we didn't have any success. I had, uh, a lady by the name Louise Delvar was my pianist. I had Duffy on sax. I had Albert Brown, a drummer. That's about all of them I can remember. I don't remember Duffy. Duffy was a saxophone player. First name, do you remember that? No. All I can remember is Duffy. Did he play alto or Ternal? Alto. So that didn't last very long, it didn't? No, we didn't make a success, no success whatsoever. So we just had to split up and get what we could. The piano player that I was playing with, Louise Delvar, she was the organist at St. Catherine's Church. Well, she just continued there. I guess that played pretty well, huh? Oh yeah. I mean, I pretty well. She was good. Was that a reading band? Oh yeah. Most of us had music. We had to read music. Just a few numbers, like people would want, like those numbers that I first called, they was by head. Old Lives of Jane and all those things. They was by head. Well, what happened after that band, do you remember? Well, after that band broke up, we didn't have anything to do and nobody was interested in organizing the band. We just played well, we could get a little job there. I think that's when I started playing a few jobs with René Perez, Kid René. Was that before depression or after? That was before depression. So you were pretty young. Oh yeah, yeah. So you started playing with René in the street. Did René's brass band read? Yeah. Oh yeah. They had music. And did you have any dance jobs with them? No, I never did play a dance job with René. How did that brass band sound with him and Buddy and you there? How would you work that out? Say the three trumpets. Well, I think it was real good. I'd play second lots of times, but I mostly preferred to lead. But by them being older musicians than me, they know it more than I know. Give them a preference, let them lead, and I'd be satisfied playing at second. Who would lead? René, Kid René. Would lead. Yeah. Well, if you had to take your choice, who would you say was better than Barrett's Buddy or René? Well, I think they're about, both of them are about the same. Buddy and René, they was, I couldn't tell what one was the best because both of them was real good trumpet players. Did you hear Louis Armstrong back in that time? I can't remember, Louis. I remember when I was a boy, the 34th of May, we'd go to Camp Chalmette. That was Armstrong Day. But I can't, he, Louis Armstrong would play for us, but I can't remember Louis. Were you playing then? Oh no, I was too young then. I was a boy then. Well, he must have been a boy too, huh? He was young because he, we'd, somehow or another, we'd get in contact with him from, from the boys' homes. That's where they'd get the band from. I think Shots was there with him too. I can't remember Shots in that time. No. No. I remember Shots seeing him around the, that story, he used to play music on that story. And the Copperators Hall, those old halls. You went to dances before you played? Oh yeah, yeah I did. Where did you? The Copperators Hall, the Economy Hall, the Roof Garden on top of the Epithian Temple a long time ago. And then we had different places would give what you call lawn parties. And it'd be in the neighborhood not too far, I'd go there. Who would be in those different halls? What you mean, the musicians? What bands? Yeah, what bands would be playing those different kinds of jobs around? Oh well they'd have sometime Shots, Rene, and that's about all. I can remember in those halls they'd have sometime, this fella from over the river, trumpet player, Sun Allen. He'd be over there in those halls sometime. Overline Allen's son? Yeah that's right. I've seen it have a contest, it'd have Celestan on one end of the hall and Sun Allen on the other side, other end. And those two bands would put on some music. Remember who won? Well no, they never would have a contest of that sort, not when I was there. They'd both have turns to play music and everybody just got along nice. Well, sometimes that's best, you know?
